options.a: Right person, drug, dose, route, time, and documentation
options.b: Right person, drug, dose, route, time, and pill color
options.c: Right person, drug, dose, room, time, and documentation
options.d: Right drug, dose, route, time, family consent, and documentation

distractorExplanations.b: Tablet appearance can change between generic manufacturers, so color is not one of the rights; the sixth right is documentation.
distractorExplanations.c: Room number is a location, not one of the rights and not a valid identifier; the missing right here is route.
distractorExplanations.d: Family consent is not one of the rights, and this list drops the right person, which is confirmed with two resident identifiers.

options.a: The resident has trouble swallowing the tablet
options.b: The resident prefers taking it in applesauce
options.c: The tablet is scored down the middle
options.d: The order and the drug form allow crush

distractorExplanations.a: Swallowing trouble is a reason to ask the nurse or pharmacist for another form; it does not make an extended-release or enteric tablet safe to crush.
distractorExplanations.b: A preference for applesauce does not change whether the drug form can be crushed; the order and the product must allow it.
distractorExplanations.c: A score line means the tablet may be split if the label allows, not that it may be crushed; some scored tablets are extended-release.

medication-aide-readiness-check-rights-0.explanation: Some forms must stay intact. This item asks: “Crushing a medication is allowed only when:”. The matching answer is: The order and the drug form allow crush — never crush XL/enteric without authority. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Never crush extended-release (XL) or enteric-coated forms without authority from the nurse or pharmacist.

options.a: The reason and the response documented per the order
options.b: A set schedule so the dose is given every four hours
options.c: Documentation of the dose time alone, since PRN reasons are verbal
options.d: The resident’s request alone, with no check of the last dose time

distractorExplanations.b: PRN means as needed within the ordered minimum interval; giving it on a fixed schedule turns it into a routine dose that was not ordered.
distractorExplanations.c: PRN documentation must record the reason given and the resident’s response, not only the time of the dose.
distractorExplanations.d: Before a PRN dose the aide checks the order’s minimum interval and maximum daily dose on the MAR, not just the request.

options.a: Room number and bed letter
options.b: The facility's two identifiers
options.c: The resident answering to their name
options.d: Name and room number on the door

distractorExplanations.a: Room and bed describe a location, not the person; residents move rooms and can sit in the wrong bed or chair.
distractorExplanations.c: Confused or hard-of-hearing residents may answer to any name; two identifiers such as name plus photo or birth date are required.
distractorExplanations.d: A door sign shows who should be in the room, not who is in front of you; room number is not an accepted identifier.

medication-aide-readiness-check-rights-0.explanation: Two IDs. This item asks: “Identifying the resident uses:”. The matching answer is: The facility's two identifiers, not 'the lady in 12'. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Location descriptions such as “the lady in 12” are never identifiers.

options.a: Give a scheduled oral med already transcribed on the MAR
options.b: Document a refusal and notify the nurse as facility policy requires
options.c: Take a new phone order for a controlled drug if the state forbids it
options.d: Report a resident’s new dizziness to the charge nurse before the next dose

distractorExplanations.a: Passing scheduled oral medications already on the MAR is the core task a trained medication aide performs.
distractorExplanations.b: Documenting refusals and notifying the nurse is part of the aide’s role, not something outside scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Observing and reporting changes in condition to the nurse is expected of a medication aide.

options.a: Acceptable if given within the shift
options.b: A wrong-dose error — report per policy
options.c: Not an error if charted on time
options.d: A timing error — report per policy

distractorExplanations.a: The allowed window is set by facility policy (commonly about an hour around the scheduled time), not the whole shift.
distractorExplanations.b: The amount given was correct; giving a drug outside its time window is a timing error, not a wrong-dose error.
distractorExplanations.c: Charting a late dose as on time falsifies the record; the late administration is still a timing error to report.

options.a: Separated and double-checked, not grabbed by memory
options.b: Stored side by side on the cart so they are easy to compare
options.c: Stored alphabetically so each one is quick to find
options.d: Relabeled by the aide in marker to tell them apart

distractorExplanations.b: Side-by-side storage is how look-alike pairs get swapped; they should be separated and flagged, not placed together.
distractorExplanations.c: Alphabetical storage often puts sound-alike names next to each other, which is exactly what LASA precautions try to prevent.
distractorExplanations.d: Aides do not alter pharmacy labels or write on tablets; LASA risk is managed with separation, alerts, and double-checks.

options.a: Whenever the resident is alert and asks to take it
options.b: If the care plan and law allow, with the checks required
options.c: If a family member stays to watch the resident take it
options.d: If the aide leaves the pills at the bedside for later

distractorExplanations.a: A request does not authorize self-administration; the resident must be assessed and the practice approved in the care plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Family supervision does not replace the care-plan assessment and facility checks required for self-administration.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving medications unattended at the bedside is not self-administration and breaks storage and observation rules.

options.a: The nostril, as ordered
options.b: The eye, if the bottle says sterile
options.c: The ear canal of both ears
options.d: The ear, as ordered

distractorExplanations.a: Otic means ear; a nasal route is a different product and order, so this is a wrong-route error.
distractorExplanations.b: Otic preparations are not made for the eye even when sterile; giving an ear drop in the eye is a serious wrong-route error.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops go only in the ear(s) named in the order; treating both ears when one is ordered is a wrong-site error.

medication-aide-readiness-check-rights-0.explanation: Route errors blind people. This item asks: “The right route for an ear drop is:”. The matching answer is: The ear, as ordered — not the eye because the bottles look alike. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Do not put ear drops in the eye just because the bottles look alike.

options.a: Do not double-dose — check the MAR and the nurse
options.b: Give it again, since a missed dose is worse than an extra
options.c: Skip it and give the next scheduled dose as a double
options.d: Ask the resident whether they already took it

distractorExplanations.b: An unconfirmed second dose risks a double dose and overdose; uncertainty means hold and check, not repeat.
distractorExplanations.c: Doubling the next dose is a dose change the aide cannot make; check the MAR and ask the nurse instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Residents may not remember accurately; the MAR and the nurse are the reliable sources for whether a dose was given.

options.a: You give it and recheck the pressure in an hour
options.b: You follow the parameter and notify as written
options.c: You give half the dose when the pressure is low
options.d: You hold it and document only at shift end

distractorExplanations.a: A hold parameter means the dose is not given when the reading is below the limit; rechecking later does not override the order.
distractorExplanations.c: Changing the dose is outside the aide’s scope; the order says hold, and the nurse is notified as written.
distractorExplanations.d: The hold must be documented when it happens and the nurse notified as the order states, not batched at shift end.

options.a: The official state medication aide certification exam
options.b: A CNA skills checklist with gait-belt and transfer tasks
options.c: Independent practice — not a CNA skills or nursing-board exam form
options.d: An NCLEX-PN style nursing-board practice form for practical nurses

distractorExplanations.a: This is an independent practice mock, not the official state certification exam or one of its forms.
distractorExplanations.b: Medication aide content covers medication administration, not CNA mobility skills such as gait-belt transfers.
distractorExplanations.d: The NCLEX-PN is the practical nurse licensing exam; this mock is independent medication aide practice.

options.a: Between the cheek and gum until dissolved
options.b: Swallowed whole with a full glass of water
options.c: Absorbed through the skin from a patch
options.d: Under the tongue until dissolved

distractorExplanations.a: Between the cheek and gum is the buccal route; sublingual means under the tongue.
distractorExplanations.b: Swallowing with water is the oral (PO) route; a sublingual tablet must dissolve under the tongue.
distractorExplanations.c: Absorption through the skin from a patch is the transdermal route, not sublingual.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: SL is not PO. This item asks: “Sublingual means:”. The matching answer is: Under the tongue until dissolved — not swallowed whole. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. A sublingual tablet is not swallowed whole.

options.a: Clean skin directly over the old patch so the dose overlaps
options.b: Clean, dry, intact skin, dated, old patch removed
options.c: The same site each time so absorption stays consistent
options.d: Skin freshly coated with lotion so the patch sticks better

distractorExplanations.a: Applying over or beside an old patch stacks the dose; the old patch must be removed before the new one goes on.
distractorExplanations.c: Sites are rotated to prevent skin irritation; reusing one site is not how consistent absorption is achieved.
distractorExplanations.d: Lotions and oils reduce adhesion and can change absorption; patches go on clean, dry, intact skin.

options.a: Place the drop directly onto the center of the cornea for best absorption
options.b: Give two different eye drops back to back so neither washes the other out
options.c: Avoid touching the dropper to the eye and wait between different drops
options.d: Use one bottle for roommates if both have the same order

distractorExplanations.a: Drops go into the lower conjunctival sac, not onto the cornea, which is sensitive and triggers blinking.
distractorExplanations.b: Giving drops back to back washes out the first; wait about five minutes between different eye drops.
distractorExplanations.d: Eye drop bottles are single-resident items; sharing spreads infection even when the orders match.

options.a: Puffs taken back to back with no wait between them
options.b: No mouth rinse after a steroid inhaler unless the resident asks for one
options.c: A shared spacer between residents if it is wiped after use
options.d: A shake/prime if the product requires it and a slow breath as taught

distractorExplanations.a: Most metered-dose inhaler instructions call for a short wait (often about a minute) between puffs.
distractorExplanations.b: Rinsing after an inhaled steroid helps prevent oral thrush and is part of correct technique, not optional.
distractorExplanations.c: Spacers are single-resident devices; wiping does not make sharing acceptable.

options.a: Unwrapped and inserted as trained, with privacy
options.b: Inserted with the foil wrapper left on for easier handling
options.c: Softened in warm water, then given by mouth
options.d: Inserted while the resident lies on the right side

distractorExplanations.b: The wrapper must be removed; a suppository left in foil cannot melt or be absorbed.
distractorExplanations.c: A rectal suppository is never given orally; if too soft it is briefly chilled, not dissolved in water.
distractorExplanations.d: The usual position is the left side-lying (Sims’) position, which follows the anatomy of the colon.

options.a: Under the tongue
options.b: Between cheek and gum
options.c: Swallowed with a sip of water
options.d: Inside the nostril

distractorExplanations.a: Under the tongue is the sublingual route; buccal means between the cheek and the gum.
distractorExplanations.c: Swallowing is the oral route; a buccal tablet stays between cheek and gum until it dissolves.
distractorExplanations.d: Inside the nostril is the intranasal route, not buccal, which refers to the cheek.

options.a: A household kitchen teaspoon
options.b: An unmarked bottle cap
options.c: An oral syringe or marked cup
options.d: An injection syringe with the needle removed

distractorExplanations.a: Household spoons vary widely in volume, so they are not accurate for measuring liquid medication doses.
distractorExplanations.b: A cap without calibrated markings cannot measure a dose accurately; use an oral syringe or marked cup.
distractorExplanations.d: Injection syringes invite wrong-route errors; ISMP recommends dedicated oral syringes for liquid oral doses.

medication-aide-readiness-check-routes-0.explanation: Oral syringes stay oral. This item asks: “A liquid oral med is measured with:”. The matching answer is: An oral syringe or marked cup, not a kitchen spoon. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Kitchen spoons are not accurate measuring devices.

options.a: A thick layer so it lasts until the next shift
options.b: Applied with a bare finger straight from the jar
options.c: Rubbed into any open wound nearby as well
options.d: A thin layer on intact skin as ordered

distractorExplanations.a: Topicals are applied thinly as ordered; a thick layer does not extend action and wastes or overdoses the drug.
distractorExplanations.b: Use gloves or an applicator and never double-dip into a shared jar; bare-finger use contaminates the product.
distractorExplanations.c: Topical medication goes only on the ordered site; open wounds need their own wound-care order.

options.a: Straight toward the septum so the spray stays inside
options.b: As the product says, usually not straight up the septum
options.c: Toward the back of the throat so it is swallowed
options.d: Into both nostrils from one bottle shared on the unit

distractorExplanations.a: Aiming at the septum irritates it and can cause nosebleeds; the tip is usually aimed toward the outer wall.
distractorExplanations.c: Nasal sprays act on the nasal lining; spraying toward the throat means the dose is swallowed instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Nasal spray bottles are single-resident items; sharing spreads infection between residents.

options.a: Within scope once the aide has watched a nurse give one
options.b: Within scope if the resident asks and consents
options.c: Usually outside medication-aide scope — do not improvise
options.d: Allowed if the nurse draws it up and hands it over

distractorExplanations.a: Observing a nurse does not expand legal scope; injections are generally outside medication aide practice.
distractorExplanations.b: Resident consent does not change the aide’s legal scope of practice, which is set by state rules.
distractorExplanations.d: A nurse preparing the syringe does not transfer authority to inject; the aide still may not give an IM injection.

options.a: Given whole with water as the order directs
options.b: Held when the resident is NPO and the nurse is told
options.c: Documented on the MAR right after the resident swallows
options.d: Opened and sprinkled unless the label says they may

distractorExplanations.a: Giving a time-release capsule whole as ordered is the correct practice, not something to avoid.
distractorExplanations.b: Holding per an NPO order and notifying the nurse is appropriate; the danger is opening the capsule.
distractorExplanations.c: Documenting right after administration is correct practice; opening and sprinkling is what should not happen.

options.a: The pinna pulled as trained for that age
options.b: The pinna pulled down and back, as for a toddler
options.c: The dropper tip inserted deep into the ear canal
options.d: The resident sitting up straight with the head level

distractorExplanations.b: Down and back straightens the ear canal in young children; in adults the pinna is pulled up and back.
distractorExplanations.c: The dropper should not enter the canal; inserting it can injure the canal and contaminate the bottle.
distractorExplanations.d: The head is tilted with the affected ear up and kept there a few minutes so the drops stay in the canal.

options.a: Meds with a full glass of juice and a light snack
options.b: Follow the exact order — not a full breakfast
options.c: Hold all scheduled meds until the resident can eat
options.d: Nothing by mouth, including meds, until the nurse says

distractorExplanations.a: NPO except meds allows meds with minimal water as ordered, not juice or food.
distractorExplanations.c: The order specifically exempts medications, so scheduled meds are still given with minimal fluid.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes strict NPO; “except meds” means ordered medications are still given by mouth.

options.a: Allowed to sleep it off alone
options.b: Given the next dose anyway
options.c: Monitored and the nurse told
options.d: Given coffee to stay awake

distractorExplanations.a: New-opioid drowsiness can precede respiratory depression; the resident needs monitoring and the nurse must be told.
distractorExplanations.b: Giving more opioid to a sedated resident adds to the risk; the nurse assesses before any further dose.
distractorExplanations.d: Caffeine does not reverse opioid sedation and hides the problem; the change must be reported to the nurse.

medication-aide-readiness-check-safety-0.explanation: Sedation stacks. This item asks: “A resident drowsy after a new opioid should be:”. The matching answer is: Monitored and the nurse told — do not give another sedative on your own. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Do not give another sedative on your own.

options.a: Given with an antihistamine already on the MAR
options.b: Held and reported as a possible allergy
options.c: Recorded as a normal side effect and given again
options.d: Given, then reported at the end of the shift

distractorExplanations.a: An antihistamine can mask an evolving allergic reaction; the antibiotic is held until the nurse assesses.
distractorExplanations.c: A new rash after a new antibiotic may be an allergy, which can escalate to anaphylaxis if the drug is repeated.
distractorExplanations.d: Possible allergic reactions are reported right away, before another dose, not at shift end.

options.a: Borrow a tablet from another cart to balance the count
options.b: Recount at the next shift change before reporting
options.c: Stop and report — do not 'fix' the book later
options.d: Correct the count sheet and explain it in a note

distractorExplanations.a: Borrowing controlled drugs hides the discrepancy and creates a second count error; stop and report.
distractorExplanations.b: Discrepancies are reported immediately so they can be investigated; waiting a shift delays the investigation.
distractorExplanations.d: Altering the count record to match is falsification; the discrepancy must be reported as found.

options.a: Giving the drug earlier in the day on your own
options.b: Raising all four bed rails so the resident stays in bed
options.c: Holding the dose whenever the resident seems sleepy
options.d: Safety measures and reporting dizziness

distractorExplanations.a: Changing administration time is a prescriber or nurse decision; the aide reports dizziness instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Full rails can act as a restraint and increase injury from climbing over them; use ordered fall precautions.
distractorExplanations.c: An aide holds a dose only per the order’s parameters; drowsiness or dizziness is reported to the nurse.

medication-aide-readiness-check-safety-0.explanation: Meds change fall risk. This item asks: “Fall risk after a night blood-pressure drug means:”. The matching answer is: Safety measures and reporting dizziness, not a secret extra pill. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Never give an extra or unordered pill to manage it.

options.a: A hazardous-drug problem — follow the special procedure
options.b: Acceptable if the aide wears a pair of exam gloves
options.c: Acceptable if the crushed powder is wiped up afterward
options.d: Acceptable because oral tablets are not hazardous drugs

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves alone do not control airborne powder; hazardous drugs are manipulated only under the special procedure.
distractorExplanations.c: Cleanup afterward does not prevent inhalation or spread of hazardous dust during crushing.
distractorExplanations.d: Many oral antineoplastics are on the NIOSH hazardous drug list and need special handling.

options.a: Is allowed if the roommate agrees to share
options.b: Is a no — only their ordered drug
options.c: Is allowed if the nurse is told afterward
options.d: Is allowed once if doses match

distractorExplanations.a: A drug dispensed for one resident cannot be given to another, even with consent; this is also diversion of a controlled drug.
distractorExplanations.c: Telling the nurse later does not make giving another resident’s opioid legal or safe; ask the nurse about the resident’s own orders.
distractorExplanations.d: Matching strength does not change ownership; each resident receives only drugs dispensed for them.

options.a: Optional if gloves are worn
options.b: Needed at shift start only
options.c: Required
options.d: Optional for oral meds

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene; hands are cleaned before putting gloves on and after taking them off.
distractorExplanations.b: Hand hygiene is repeated before and after each resident contact, not done once at the start of the shift.
distractorExplanations.d: Oral meds are handled and taken by mouth, so hand hygiene matters as much as for any other route.

options.a: Mixed ahead of time for the whole hallway
options.b: Mixed with all of that resident’s meds in one spoonful
options.c: Saved in the cart for the next scheduled dose
options.d: Given to that one resident, not a shared cup

distractorExplanations.a: Premixing for several residents breaks identification and timing; each dose is prepared for one resident at a time.
distractorExplanations.b: Crushed medications are generally given separately unless the pharmacist approves mixing, because of interaction and dosing concerns.
distractorExplanations.c: Crushed doses are given right away; saved mixtures lose identity and stability and must be discarded per policy.

options.a: Discard per policy and get a replacement
options.b: Wipe it off and give it if it landed on a clean floor
options.c: Return it to the blister pack for the pharmacy
options.d: Give it, then report the contamination

distractorExplanations.b: A dropped tablet is contaminated regardless of how clean the floor looks; it is discarded per policy.
distractorExplanations.c: Returning a contaminated tablet to packaging risks another resident receiving it; discard and document instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Reporting does not make giving a contaminated tablet acceptable; get a replacement first.

medication-aide-readiness-check-safety-0.explanation: Floor pills are dirty. This item asks: “If you drop a tablet on the floor:”. The matching answer is: Discard per policy and get a replacement — do not blow it off and give it. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Do not blow off a dropped tablet and give it.

options.a: Drugs the aide should hold for any resident over age 65 until reviewed
options.b: A reason the nurse/pharmacist watches — you give only as ordered
options.c: Banned in nursing homes under federal regulations
options.d: A reason to cut the dose in half for residents over age 75

distractorExplanations.a: Beers criteria flag drugs for prescriber and pharmacist review; an aide may not hold an ordered drug because of age.
distractorExplanations.c: The Beers criteria are expert guidance on potentially inappropriate drugs, not a federal ban.
distractorExplanations.d: Dose changes are a prescriber decision; the aide gives the dose as ordered and reports side effects.

options.a: Water to help wash the pill down
options.b: Time alone to cough it up in private
options.c: Emergency response — do not leave them
options.d: A finger sweep to find the pill blindly

distractorExplanations.a: Fluids poured into a blocked airway can worsen choking or cause aspiration; call for emergency help.
distractorExplanations.b: A choking resident must not be left alone; stay, call for help, and start the emergency response.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; follow the trained choking emergency response instead.

options.a: Locked at the end of each med pass
options.b: Keys left in the lock during the pass
options.c: Unlocked in the dining room at meals
options.d: Locked when out of your sight

distractorExplanations.a: The cart must be locked whenever it leaves the aide’s sight, including during the pass, not just when it ends.
distractorExplanations.b: Keys left in the lock make the cart effectively unlocked; keys stay on the aide’s person.
distractorExplanations.c: A cart left unlocked in a common area invites diversion and accidental ingestion by residents.

options.a: When in doubt, report — do not wait for 'bad enough'
options.b: Report only effects that are not listed on the label
options.c: Report once the effect lasts longer than a day
options.d: Report at the next care-plan meeting

distractorExplanations.b: Listed side effects can still be severe or new for that resident; if in doubt, report it.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting a day can let a serious reaction progress; possible adverse effects are reported when noticed.
distractorExplanations.d: Care-plan meetings are too late for a possible adverse reaction; the nurse is told right away.

options.a: Before the pass, to save time later
options.b: After the drug is taken
options.c: At the end of the shift for all meds
options.d: When it is poured

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-charting records doses that may be refused, held, or dropped, which falsifies the MAR.
distractorExplanations.c: Batch charting at shift end risks errors and leaves the MAR inaccurate for others during the shift.
distractorExplanations.d: Pouring is not administration; the dose is documented after the resident actually takes it.

medication-aide-readiness-check-docs-046.explanation: Chart what occurred. This item asks: “Documentation happens:”. The matching answer is: After the drug is taken, not before you walk in the room. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Never document before you walk into the room.

options.a: Held, since the dose was not given
options.b: Omitted, and retried at the next scheduled time
options.c: Refused, with the nurse notified as required
options.d: Refused, with crushing in food tried next

distractorExplanations.a: “Held” is for doses withheld under a parameter or nurse decision; a refusal has its own code and notification.
distractorExplanations.b: Retrying at the next scheduled time can double-dose; the refusal is charted and the nurse decides what follows.
distractorExplanations.d: Hiding a refused drug in food is covert administration, which violates resident rights without a specific order and plan.

medication-aide-readiness-check-docs-047.explanation: Refusals are data. This item asks: “A refusal is charted as:”. The matching answer is: Refused, with the nurse notified as required — not a secret skip. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. A refusal is never a secret skip.

options.a: Timed at the scheduled hour to match the MAR
options.b: Corrected with correction fluid over the old time
options.c: Left blank so the next shift can complete it
options.d: Honest and timed as a late entry

distractorExplanations.a: Recording the scheduled time instead of the actual time backdates the entry and falsifies the record.
distractorExplanations.b: Correction fluid obscures the original entry; errors get a single line, initials, and the correct information.
distractorExplanations.c: Only the person who gave the dose documents it; another shift cannot chart care it did not provide.

medication-aide-readiness-check-docs-048.explanation: Falsifying time is a legal issue. This item asks: “Late entry on the MAR must be:”. The matching answer is: Honest and timed as a late entry, not backdated as on-time. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. It is never backdated to look on time.

options.a: A new medical diagnosis they invented
options.b: A refusal they witnessed during the pass
options.c: A pulse they took before digoxin
options.d: A dose they held per the written parameter

distractorExplanations.b: Documenting a refusal the aide witnessed is required, not prohibited.
distractorExplanations.c: Recording a pulse the aide is permitted to take before a drug like digoxin is part of the task.
distractorExplanations.d: A dose held under the written parameter must be documented by the aide who held it.

options.a: A note in the MAR without a second person
options.b: A witness and the form your facility uses
options.c: Flushing right away, with the count fixed later
options.d: Return to the cart drawer for the next dose

distractorExplanations.a: Controlled-drug waste requires a second witness who co-signs; a solo MAR note does not meet that standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Waste is documented with a witness at the time it happens; fixing the count later hides discrepancies.
distractorExplanations.d: A dose that has been prepared or contaminated is wasted with a witness, not returned to stock.

options.a: Hold all meds until the system is restored
options.b: Give from memory and chart everything later
options.c: Use the downtime paper process
options.d: Use yesterday’s printout as today’s MAR

distractorExplanations.a: Downtime does not justify missing doses; the paper downtime MAR lets the pass continue safely.
distractorExplanations.b: Memory-based passes cause omissions and wrong doses; downtime forms are used during the pass.
distractorExplanations.d: An old printout may miss new, changed, or stopped orders; use the facility’s current downtime record.

medication-aide-readiness-check-docs-051.explanation: Downtime procedures exist. This item asks: “If the eMAR is down, you:”. The matching answer is: Use the downtime paper process — you do not skip the pass. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. The medication pass is not skipped.

options.a: Morphine can be given without checking, since it differs
options.b: The allergy can be ignored if the rash was years ago
options.c: Codeine cough syrups are fine, since the allergy was to tablets
options.d: You still check every pass and report a new reaction

distractorExplanations.a: Opioids can cross-react; any related drug is checked against the allergy with the nurse before giving it.
distractorExplanations.b: Allergies stay on the record and are checked every pass regardless of when the reaction happened.
distractorExplanations.c: The allergy is to the drug, not the dosage form; codeine in a syrup carries the same risk.

options.a: Reported at once so the resident can be checked
options.b: Reported at the end of the shift on the form
options.c: Corrected by skipping the next scheduled dose
options.d: Reported only if the resident shows symptoms

distractorExplanations.b: Medication errors are reported at once so the resident can be assessed; the incident form follows, it does not replace reporting.
distractorExplanations.c: Adjusting later doses is a nurse or prescriber decision; the error is reported so they can decide.
distractorExplanations.d: Effects may be delayed, so every error is reported whether or not symptoms appear.

options.a: Fine if it is closed after the pass
options.b: A privacy risk only if names show
options.c: A privacy and diversion risk
options.d: Fine while the aide is in a nearby room

distractorExplanations.a: An open MAR in a public lobby exposes resident information while it sits there, even if closed later.
distractorExplanations.b: The MAR shows drug and resident details that identify people and reveal controlled drugs, beyond names alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving the MAR out of sight in a public area is exactly when privacy and diversion risks occur.

options.a: Read the list to any relative who visits often
options.b: Hand them a printed copy of the MAR
options.c: Tell them the list if they say they are family
options.d: Follow facility privacy rules

distractorExplanations.a: Frequent visits do not make a relative authorized; disclosure follows the resident’s wishes and facility privacy rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Releasing a copy of the MAR is a records disclosure that goes through the nurse and facility process, not the aide.
distractorExplanations.c: Claiming to be family is not verification of authority; follow privacy rules and involve the nurse.

medication-aide-readiness-check-docs-056.explanation: Privacy + the nurse. This item asks: “A family asks 'what pills is dad on?'”. The matching answer is: Follow facility privacy rules — do not recite the MAR in the hall. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official medication aide paper. Never recite the MAR in the hall; refer the family to the nurse.

options.a: Residents and your license
options.b: The pharmacy’s billing records
options.c: The outgoing shift alone
options.d: Only the facility’s inventory

distractorExplanations.b: Shift counts exist to detect loss or diversion that harms residents, not to support pharmacy billing.
distractorExplanations.c: Counts protect both shifts and, above all, residents; they are not just a release for the outgoing staff.
distractorExplanations.d: Inventory matters, but the main purpose is resident safety and accountability for each staff member’s license.

options.a: Use it after reading the package insert
options.b: Do not use it — get training or the nurse
options.c: Let the resident guide you through the dose
options.d: Use it after watching a video on your phone

distractorExplanations.a: Reading an insert is not competency validation; the aide needs facility training or the nurse.
distractorExplanations.c: Relying on the resident mid-dose shifts responsibility and risks a dosing error; get training or the nurse.
distractorExplanations.d: A video is not a validated competency check; devices like insulin pens require documented training.

options.a: A reminder list the aide may discard after the shift
options.b: The pharmacy’s order form for refills
options.c: The prescriber’s original order for each drug
options.d: The legal record of what was given

distractorExplanations.a: The MAR is a permanent part of the medical record and is retained, not a personal reminder to discard.
distractorExplanations.b: Refill requests use pharmacy processes; the MAR documents what was actually administered.
distractorExplanations.c: The original order lives in the chart; the MAR is the transcribed administration record of what was given.
